notes: Hague Convention wrongful retention; Article 13(b) defence resolved by undertakings and return order.

enrichment.short_title: Re E: Hague return to Spain with Article 13 undertakings

statutes_considered.title: Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction 1980

key_facts: E, aged 7, was retained in England by her mother at the end of the 2004 school term rather than returned to her father in Spain under a Spanish provisional measures order.
The unmarried British parents had a history of cross-border proceedings, including the father's September 2003 snatching of E and a consent order returning her to Spain.
The Granada court had awarded shared care and custody and later made an Article 15 declaration that retention in England was wrongful.
The mother relied on Article 13(b), citing the father's past conduct, her Crohn's disease and risk that E would be left with a scarcely known father if she needed surgery in England.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Hague Convention application for summary return after an Article 15 request to the Spanish authorities.
enrichment.outcome: Order for E's return to Spain on terms of detailed undertakings limiting immediate enforcement, protecting contact and suspending punitive proceedings pending a full inter partes hearing in Granada.
enrichment.ratio: Breach of rights of custody under a clear Spanish provisional measures order suffices for Article 3 wrongful retention; the English court should not go behind a competent foreign custody court's orders in summary Hague proceedings, and Article 13(b) intolerability may be managed by tailored undertakings pending welfare reconsideration in the state of habitual residence.
legal_issues: Whether retention at the end of the London school term breached the father's and Spanish court's rights of custody
Whether Spanish personal law under the Civil Code required application of English parental responsibility law
The status and effect of the Article 15 declaration
Whether return would expose E to grave risk or an intolerable situation under Article 13(b)

Re H (Abduction: Rights of Custody) [2000] 2 AC 291

notes: Interim media injunction refused; capacity and best interests tests under inherent jurisdiction and section 12 HRA.

enrichment.short_title: E v Channel Four: refusal to restrain DID documentary broadcast

statutes_considered.title: Chronically Sick and Disabled Persons Act 1970
National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: The Official Solicitor and St Helens Borough Council sought an interim injunction to stop Channel Four and the Sunday Times broadcasting a documentary about E, a 32-year-old woman with learning disability and dissociative identity disorder.
E had consented to filming and strongly wished the programme to be shown; her foster carer Judy and several clinicians supported broadcast.
Experts disagreed on whether E lacked capacity to consent to broadcast and whether publication was contrary to her best interests.
The film recorded intimate medical, social care and abuse history details that the Official Solicitor said would cause harm and breach confidence and Article 8.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent interim application in the inherent jurisdiction to restrain broadcast pending trial, with permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.outcome: Interim injunction refused; the court was not satisfied the Official Solicitor was likely to establish lack of capacity or that non-broadcast was in E's best interests at trial.
enrichment.ratio: Where an incapable adult's broadcast consent is in issue, the court asks whether capacity is lacking, whether non-broadcast is in best interests and, if needed, balances Article 8 against Article 10; under section 12(3) HRA the applicant must show a likelihood of success at trial, here not met on capacity or best interests.
legal_issues: Whether E lacked capacity to consent to broadcast of the finished documentary
Whether restraining broadcast was in E's best interests having regard to her wishes
Application of Campbell confidence and Article 8 private life protection to medical and care information
The section 12(3) threshold for interim restraint of media publication
linked_authorities: Campbell v MGN Ltd [2004] UKHL 22
Cream Holdings Ltd v Banerjee [2004] UKHL 44
Sheffield City Council v E [2004] EWHC 2808 (Fam)

notes: Local government ethics appeal; Article 10 engaged but sanction reduced from disqualification to partial suspension.

enrichment.short_title: Sanders v Kingston: councillor code breach and Article 10 sanction
key_facts: Mr Sanders, former Conservative leader of Peterborough City Council, responded offensively to Carrickfergus Borough Council's request for support for an inquiry into a soldier's death.
His handwritten notes and media interviews caused widespread condemnation; the council removed him as leader and Conservative Party figures disowned his remarks.
A Case Tribunal found breaches of paragraphs 2(b) and 4 of the model code of conduct and disqualified him from office for two years.
Sanders appealed under section 79(15), arguing Article 10 protected his speech and the code was insufficiently precise.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal to the High Court against a Standards Board Case Tribunal decision on code of conduct breaches and sanction.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed on breach findings but upheld on sanction; two-year disqualification substituted with one-year partial suspension from the office of council leader.
enrichment.ratio: Article 10 is engaged when a councillor is penalised for speech, but personal abuse and disrespectful official correspondence are not political expression entitled to heightened protection; code restrictions may be justified under Article 10(2), yet disqualifying a councillor re-elected after the events overrides the electorate and requires a proportionate sanction such as partial suspension.
legal_issues: Whether the Case Tribunal adequately considered Article 10
Whether paragraphs 2(b) and 4 were prescribed by law and sufficiently certain
Whether Sanders's statements were political expression or personal abuse
Whether two-year disqualification was a wrong exercise of the sanction discretion
linked_authorities: Hashman v United Kingdom (2000) 30 EHRR 241
Lingens v Austria (1986) 8 EHRR 407
R (pro-life) v BBC [2003] UKHL 23

notes: ASBO appeal procedure; consent below does not bar Crown Court merits rehearing.

enrichment.short_title: R (T) v Manchester Crown Court: ASBO appeal cannot be struck out for consent
key_facts: T, aged 14, did not oppose the making of an ASBO before a district judge while represented, but his mother later sought to appeal.
Mr Recorder Farley QC struck out the Crown Court appeal on the basis that consent below barred further challenge, analogising to a guilty plea.
The ASBO contained broad prohibitions on anti-social conduct, abusive language, association and entering defined areas.
Manchester City Council had raised the preliminary point; the Department for Constitutional Affairs did not oppose relief.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a Crown Court decision striking out an ASBO appeal for alleged consent at first instance.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; the Recorder's decision quashed and the appeal ordered to be reheard before a differently constituted Crown Court.
enrichment.ratio: An ASBO cannot be made merely on a defendant's consent; the court must be satisfied to the criminal standard on anti-social conduct and exercise its own necessity judgment, and on a Crown Court rehearing prior consent is relevant evidence but does not deprive the court of jurisdiction to decide the appeal on its merits.
legal_issues: Whether an ASBO may validly be founded on consent alone
Whether consent at magistrates' level bars a Crown Court ASBO appeal
The correct test when striking out an appeal for prior consent
Interaction of parental compliance and public interest in ASBO proceedings

notes: Money laundering conspiracy appeals allowed after Montila/Harmer analysis of mental element.

enrichment.short_title: R v Ali, Hussain and Khan: conspiracy to launder drug proceeds
key_facts: Ali, Hussain and Khan were convicted of conspiracies to conceal or remove bank notes suspected to be another person's drug trafficking proceeds through Watan Travel's Hawala money transfer business.
Large sums in cash were allegedly laundered between 1997 and 2001; defendants said transfers were legitimate remittances abroad.
The jury were directed they could convict if defendants only suspected the money was criminal proceeds.
Shahid Bhatti separately appealed against related conspiracy convictions from a later trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals against conviction by leave of the single judge in long-running Customs and Excise money laundering prosecutions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals allowed; convictions quashed because the jury should not have been directed that suspicion alone sufficed without proof the money was in fact proceeds of drug trafficking or other criminal conduct.
enrichment.ratio: Following Montila and Harmer, a conspiracy to contravene section 49 DTA 1994 or section 93C CJA 1988 requires proof that the property was another person's proceeds of crime, not merely that the defendant suspected or had reasonable grounds to suspect; section 1(2) Criminal Law Act 1977 applies to the mental element of the underlying offence.
legal_issues: Whether suspicion or reasonable grounds to suspect sufficed for conspiracy convictions
Effect of House of Lords decision in Montila on trial directions
Whether Harmer correctly states the law post-Montila
Use of conspiracy counts rather than substantive laundering offences
linked_authorities: R v Montila [2004] UKHL 50
R v Harmer [2005] EWCA Crim 1
R v Singh [2003] EWCA Crim 402

notes: Trial of interim PHA and restrictive covenant orders; harassment injunction continued, narrow covenant defect found.

enrichment.short_title: First Global Locums v Cosias: harassment and employment restraints upheld
key_facts: First Global Locums summarily dismissed recruitment consultant Cosias after violent and threatening conduct in the office and at a dismissal meeting.
Without-notice orders had restrained harassment under the 1997 Act and enforcement of post-termination covenants.
The judge found Cosias's evidence unreliable and accepted the claimants' account of intimidation, threats and attempts to damage the business.
Cosias challenged the validity of confidentiality and non-compete clauses and sought damages on the cross-undertaking.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Expedited trial to determine whether interim harassment and restrictive covenant injunctions were correctly granted.
enrichment.outcome: Harassment injunction continued for 24 months; confidentiality and most restrictive covenants upheld as reasonable, but the 'solicit any Client' restraint was too wide and struck from the order.
enrichment.ratio: A course of threatening and abusive conduct after dismissal may warrant a time-limited PHA injunction; an employer may protect confidential locum database information and client goodwill by tailored post-termination covenants, but a blanket prohibition on soliciting any client defined to include entire local authorities is unreasonable.
legal_issues: Whether Cosias's conduct amounted to harassment warranting continuing injunction
Whether summary dismissal for gross misconduct defeated covenant enforcement
Reasonableness of confidentiality and non-solicitation covenants in recruitment agency context
Appropriate duration of PHA orders where risk is impulsive rather than long-term
linked_authorities: Dawnay, Day & Co Ltd v De Braconier D'Alfhen [1997] IRLR 285
Faccenda Chicken Ltd v Fowler [1987] 1 Ch 117

notes: Section 94 certification quashed; Kosovo witness protection claim arguable despite post-decision prosecutor letter.

enrichment.short_title: Djakija v SSHD: quashing clearly unfounded certification for Kosovo witness
key_facts: The claimant, a Kosovan Albanian, claimed asylum after giving evidence linking Agron Zeqiri to his brother's 1999 murder by KLA forces.
He had received 24-hour police protection as a vulnerable witness at trial, but Zeqiri was acquitted and the Secretary of State certified the claim clearly unfounded.
Other family members remained in Kosovo without reported harm, but the claimant argued his evidence uniquely exposed him to reprisals.
A May 2005 prosecutor's letter recorded intimidation of the victim's family and an appeal against acquittal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Substantive judicial review of a section 94(2) clearly unfounded certificate removing in-country appeal rights.
enrichment.outcome: Certification quashed; the claim held arguable on sufficiency of future state protection and the Secretary of State ordered to treat the claim as not clearly unfounded.
enrichment.ratio: Certification requires that no legitimate view could succeed; where a witness previously needed special protection and post-acquittal protection remains unclear, especially without Home Office enquiry, the claim that return would expose him to risk beyond the general Kosovan population is at least arguable and cannot be certified.
legal_issues: Application of the section 94 clearly unfounded test after Yogathas and L
Whether the claimant's trial evidence distinguished his risk from that of other family members
Sufficiency of state protection on return to Kosovo
Effect of post-decision prosecutor evidence on certification review

notes: Youth Court mode of trial guidance; wrong threshold and clerk procedure criticised.

enrichment.short_title: CPS v Redbridge Youth Court: declining jurisdiction under section 24
key_facts: BS, aged 17, faced numerous grave either-way sexual and communications offences against a younger child, including mentor abuse and use of threats.
Redbridge Youth Court accepted jurisdiction despite CPS application to decline it, relying on comparators attracting sentences below two years.
The court applied a 'substantially in excess of two years' test and received clerk advice in private on sentencing precedents.
On a later hearing the court refused to reopen its mode of trial decision when further charges were added.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Agreed judicial review by the Crown Prosecution Service to quash Youth Court mode of trial decisions accepting jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Both Youth Court decisions quashed; matter remitted for reconsideration applying the real prospect of section 91 long-term detention test.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 24 MCA 1980 a Youth Court should not decline jurisdiction unless there is a real prospect that, if convicted, a section 91 PCCSA 2000 long custodial sentence may be passed; the test is not whether a sentence substantially exceeding two years is likely, and clerks must not advise benches in private on precedents without parties' input.
legal_issues: Correct threshold for declining jurisdiction under section 24
Whether section 91 long-term detention was a realistic possibility for a 17-year-old defendant
Propriety of clerk giving private legal advice and case citations to the bench
Whether the court could reopen an earlier mode of trial decision under section 25

notes: ASBO 'any criminal offence' prohibition held plainly invalid; Boddington applies to breach proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: R (W) v DPP: invalid ASBO clause prohibiting any criminal offence
key_facts: W, aged 14, was subject to a two-year ASBO with six prohibitions including a ban on committing any criminal offence.
He admitted shoplifting sweets and Lucozade and was convicted of theft and breaching the ASBO; he received a conditional discharge for theft and absolute discharge for breach.
Youth Court proceedings were stated to the High Court on whether the blanket criminal-offence clause was valid.
The ASBO also contained tailored restrictions on entering an area, intimidation, vehicle interference and nuisance behaviour.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from Preston Youth Court convictions for ASBO breach and theft.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; clause 6 held plainly too wide and invalid, so the breach conviction could not stand and the matter was remitted to magistrates.
enrichment.ratio: An ASBO must be expressed in terms a defendant can understand and be no wider than necessary; a prohibition on committing any criminal offence is unenforceably vague and disproportionate, and magistrates may consider plain invalidity in breach proceedings without prior variation proceedings.
legal_issues: Whether an ASBO may prohibit all criminal conduct
Clarity and proportionality requirements for ASBO terms
Whether breach proceedings may challenge validity of the underlying order
Relationship between ASBO breach and substantive criminal charges

Boddington v British Transport Police [1999] 2 AC 143
R v P (Shane Tony) [2004] EWCA Crim 287

notes: Renewed JR permission refused; further representations did not amount to fresh asylum claim.

enrichment.short_title: Tchunuangang v SSHD: refusal of fresh claim on Cameroon political activity
key_facts: The claimant, a Cameroonian, claimed asylum in 1999; his claim and appeal were dismissed in 2001-2002.
After returning and making a second claim in 2003, he was again refused and an adjudicator rejected his account of arrest and ill-treatment.
Further 2004 representations relied on SDF UK and CDC membership cards, embassy demonstration photographs and a prison conditions report.
The Secretary of State treated the material as not sufficiently different to constitute a fresh claim warranting a new appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review of refusal to treat further representations as a fresh asylum claim.
enrichment.outcome: Permission refused; the court held the Secretary of State's fresh-claim assessment was reasonable and no arguable ground for review existed.
enrichment.ratio: Further representations constitute a fresh claim only if sufficiently different that an adjudicator might reasonably take a favourable view; post-adjudication political membership and demonstration evidence that could have been put at the earlier hearing, together with a general prison conditions report irrelevant to a claimant not at risk of arrest, does not meet that test.
legal_issues: Correct legal test for a fresh asylum claim after prior refusal
Whether SDF UK and CDC membership and embassy protest evidence were new and material
Admissibility of documents predating the adjudicator hearing
Relevance of general country prison conditions evidence
